clinicalPearls: Congenital failure of the posterior nasal aperture to canalise, leaving a bony, membranous, or mixed obstruction between the nasal cavity and nasopharynx
Bilateral atresia is a neonatal airway emergency because neonates are obligate nasal breathers, producing cyclical cyanosis relieved by crying
Unilateral atresia often presents later in childhood with persistent unilateral nasal obstruction and discharge
Failure to pass a fine catheter through the nose and absence of misting on a cold mirror suggest the diagnosis
CT best characterises whether the obstruction is bony, membranous, or mixed and guides surgical planning
Association with CHARGE and other syndromes means a bilateral case warrants a search for additional anomalies
The immediate priority in a bilateral case is to establish an oral airway, classically with an oral airway device or feeding-teat adaptation, before definitive surgical repair
reference.pathophysiology: Choanal atresia results from persistence of tissue that should break down during development of the posterior nasal apertures, leaving the choana occluded by bone, membrane, or a combination of the two. Several embryological explanations have been proposed, including failure of rupture of the bucconasal membrane and abnormal mesodermal persistence. Because newborns preferentially breathe through the nose, complete bilateral obstruction prevents effective nasal airflow, so the infant becomes cyanotic at rest and improves paradoxically when crying opens the mouth, giving the classic cyclical pattern. In unilateral disease the patent side maintains the airway, and the condition presents insidiously with chronic one-sided obstruction and discharge.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal nasal obstruction from mucosal oedema or rhinitis
additionalInvestigations: Attempted passage of a fine catheter through each nostril and the cold-mirror misting test at the cot side
Flexible nasal endoscopy to inspect the posterior nasal cavity
CT of the nose and skull base to define the nature and thickness of the atretic plate
Assessment for CHARGE and other syndromic associations, including cardiac and ophthalmological review
Genetic evaluation where a syndrome is suspected
redFlags: Cyclical cyanosis relieved by crying in a neonate, indicating bilateral atresia and an airway emergency
Respiratory distress and feeding difficulty in the newborn
Features suggesting CHARGE association such as coloboma, cardiac, or ear anomalies
Failure to establish or maintain an adequate oral airway
reference.prognosis: With prompt airway management and surgical repair the outlook is good, though restenosis can occur and may require revision, and prognosis in bilateral cases is influenced by any associated syndromic anomalies.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise bilateral atresia promptly in a distressed neonate and delaying airway support
Attributing unilateral discharge and obstruction in a child to infection rather than investigating for atresia
Overlooking CHARGE and other syndromic associations in bilateral cases
Underestimating the risk of postoperative restenosis and not planning appropriate follow-up
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Secure the neonatal airway urgently in bilateral atresia with an oral airway or modified McGovern nipple, or intubation, since neonates are obligate nasal breathers
Definitive treatment is surgical perforation of the atretic plate, usually by transnasal endoscopic drilling of the bony or membranous obstruction with restoration of choanal patency
Maintain post-operative patency with nasal stenting, saline irrigation and topical decongestant or steroid measures, with regular debridement
Undertake surveillance nasendoscopy for restenosis, with dilatation, revision surgery or topical mitomycin application where re-stenosis recurs
Support feeding and growth with nasogastric or careful oral feeding until the airway is secured
Screen bilateral cases for CHARGE and other syndromes with cardiology, ophthalmology and genetic evaluation
Manage within a paediatric ENT, neonatology and anaesthetic multidisciplinary team
